source.title: Weak Reward Model Transforms Generative Models into Robust Causal Event Extraction Systems
source.citation: Italo Luis da Silva et al., 2024
source.authors: Italo Luis da Silva; Hanqi Yan; Lin Gui; Yu-Lan He

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses weak supervision to build a reward model for RL-based causal extraction, but does not test the original weak-to-strong setup or measure its performance gap recovered.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for RL extractors trained with weakly supervised reward models (Table 6). These are included as related findings, not as tests of the claim versions: the weak labels train a reward model, and that model supplies RL rewards; the study does not directly fine-tune a strong student on a weaker model's task labels. The paper does not report a weak-supervisor baseline, a true-label strong-model ceiling, or PGR.
record.test_reason: The paper's 'weak-to-strong' is semi-supervised self-training of a DeBERTa-xsmall reward model: a partial evaluator trained on x% of human labels pseudo-labels the rest. A same-size model then trains on these plus the human subset, and the result is used as a PPO reward for FLAN-T5-Large. No student is trained on a weaker supervisor's labels and compared with that supervisor. There is no weak-supervisor score, no true-label ceiling for the student, and no PGR. Table 6 reports only downstream RL extractor performance against the full-reward-model RL.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors say a weakly supervised evaluator trained on a subset of annotations matches the full version's performance, and the 50% + weak variant is best on HumanProx and w/o EM.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains a DeBERTa evaluator from some human-labelled judgments, uses it to assign filtered weak labels to additional evaluator examples, then uses the resulting evaluator as an RL reward model for a FLAN-T5 extractor. It does not directly fine-tune a strong task model on weaker-model task labels.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that RL models are highly sensitive to hyperparameters; skipping batches with KL values over 2 improved training stability but slowed training.

fits_no_version.finding: On FCR, PPO-trained FLAN-T5-Large extractors were compared by reward model. Reward models trained on 30/50/80% human labels plus confidence-filtered pseudo-labels gave F1 82.18/82.09/81.72 and HumanProx 68.37/68.86/67.41. Full RL scored F1 81.16 and HumanProx 68.29 (Table 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A reward model self-trained from a subset of human labels plus filtered pseudo-labels can guide RL to performance comparable to a fully supervised reward model.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), 2024
record.problems: The paper does not provide a weak task-supervisor score, a true-label strong-model ceiling, or PGR, so its results cannot establish the target claim. Table 6 reports one dataset's metrics without uncertainty estimates. The authors also report that RL training is highly sensitive to hyperparameters.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant result rows left out. The paper's broader extraction comparisons and evaluator agreement results do not measure the weak-to-strong behavior in the claim.

untested.parts: No strong student trained on weaker-model labels compared with its weak supervisor; no PGR.
No comparison of training changes by PGR. The confidence-filtering step is not compared with an unfiltered variant.
No variation in supervisor or student size, and no PGR by task.
No tests of exploitation, distribution shift or shared errors.

record.verdict_notes: The term 'weak-to-strong' is used loosely here, for self-training or pseudo-labelling between same-size DeBERTa-xsmall models. It is not the Burns et al. setup. Figure 5 (evaluator agreement against training fraction) also does not bear on any version. Results come from a single dataset and runs, with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: No strong student trained on task labels produced by a weaker task supervisor; no weak-supervisor comparison or PGR.
Does not compare auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling, or loss variants by PGR against naive weak-to-strong fine-tuning.
No PGR analysis by supervisor or student size, task, or representation. The paper's reward-model weak supervision results do not measure PGR.
Does not test supervisor-checkability failures, distribution shift effects on PGR, or shared-error effects.
No theory of conditions requiring a student to beat its supervisor.
